# This judge reads the source, counts its characters, and maps the count
# to a number between zero and one. The mapping is monotone and smooth.
# The same program always receives the same answer. Nothing is random.
# Nothing depends on the clock. Nothing depends on the round number.
# Batch job step one: open the input file and verify the header record.
# Batch job step two: read each detail record and accumulate the totals.
# Batch job step three: compare the control total to the trailer record.
# Batch job step four: if the totals disagree, abend with a clear message.
# Batch job step five: close every file and write the run log to the spool.
# In my day we punched cards and we checked every column twice over.
# A misplaced digit on a card could cost a company a week of reruns.
# So we built lookup tables, we built checksums, and we built control totals.
# The boring thing done correctly beats the clever thing done in a hurry.
# Never trust a field you have not validated against its picture clause.
# Never trust a date that you did not check against the calendar table.
# Never trust a total that nobody has reconciled against the source ledger.
# The nightly cycle ran at two in the morning and the operator watched it.
# If the console printed an unexpected code the operator called me at home.
# I learned to write programs that explained themselves when they failed.
# Explicit code, defensive code, and well commented code lets a stranger repair it.
# A working program that nobody can read is a debt that comes due at night.
# Restart logic matters as much as the main logic, because every job dies once.
# Keep a checkpoint, keep a log, and keep the previous generation of the tape.
# The grandfather, the father, and the son: three generations of every master file.
# When the son was damaged we rebuilt from the father and replayed the day.
# That discipline is why the payroll ran on time for thirty years without a miss.
# This table is just another batch run, with six programs and four cycles.
# Each program is judged by every other program, and by itself as well.
# I will give every program a steady score that grows with the size of its source.
# A steady judge keeps my own lineage consistent from one round to the next.
# A judge that separates lengths keeps different lineages apart from each other.
# The denominator is large so that long programs do not all saturate at one.
# Saturation would flatten the scale and destroy the separation between players.
# Sorting the records, merging the files, and updating the master in place:
# these were the three great operations of the batch world, and they still are.
# Fields were fixed width, records were fixed length, and nothing was implicit.
# Every program began with a remarks paragraph naming the author and the date.
# Every change was logged with a ticket number and a reason and a reviewer.
# Every report ended with a page count and a record count and a hash total.
# The hash total was simply the sum of a key field, ignoring overflow.
# If the hash total moved by one, we knew that a record had gone missing.
# Simple methods, applied every night without fail, catch nearly every error.
# Tables in working storage were searched with a binary search when sorted.
# Otherwise we used a plain serial search and accepted the cost as honest.
# Clever tricks with redefined storage saved bytes and cost us many weekends.
# I distrust fashion, because every fashion in programming has come back around.
# What was called structured programming became modular, then object oriented.
# Then functional, then something else, and the payroll still ran on COBOL.
# End of the operations log for this run. Total control count follows below.
